entities.summary: Monism is an ancient philosophical concept attributed to the Greek philosopher, Xenophanes (c. 570–479 BCE), who posited that a single, unified reality underlies all existence. This idea gained prominence in Neoplatonism, where the One, a singular, eternal, and unchanging reality, was seen as the source of all being. Monism asserts that existence is fundamentally one, and various kinds of monism can be distinguished, including priority monism, which posits a distinct source prior to all existence, and existence monism, which posits a single, universal entity. Monism has had significant repercussions in the development of Western philosophy, influencing thinkers such as Plato and Aristotle. Its influence can also be seen in the works of modern philosophers, such as Bertrand Russell, who discussed monism in relation to the nature of reality and knowledge. The concept of monism has been explored in various philosophical traditions, including existentialism and postmodernism, and continues to be a topic of debate among philosophers and scholars today.
